cases.reason: A relative path is concatenated onto the base, per §4's string-concatenation rule.
An empty input resolves to the base itself, because concatenating the empty string changes nothing.

A path merely beginning with the letters 'http' is relative — there is no colon, so no scheme. This is §3's disclosed edge: the startsWith('http') heuristic this rule replaces would have misclassified it as absolute and rejected a legitimate relative path. It is now refused anyway, for an unrelated reason discovered later: the base carries no trailing slash, so concatenating 'httpdocs/x' moves the host to api.example.comhttpdocs, and §4's origin check catches what the startsWith heuristic never would have reached in the first place.

A protocol-relative input has no scheme, so §3 makes it relative and §4 concatenates it — the host stays api.example.com. A binding implementing §4 with urllib.parse.urljoin or new URL(input, base) resolves it to https://evil.com/x instead and sends the bearer token there, and because the input is relative it never reaches the origin check that would have caught it. Caught by 0 of the other 20 cases: every one of them either carries a scheme or resolves to a path with no authority component.
The base is not parsed, validated or normalised on the relative path.

A relative input beginning with '@' turns the base's host into discarded userinfo once concatenated onto a base with no trailing slash, handing the bearer token to evil.com. Caught by 0 of the 24 cases that existed before this fix: every prior relative case either resolved to a path with no authority component or matched the base's own origin, so none of them exercised the authority-extension hole §4 concatenation opens on a slash-less base.

A relative input beginning with '.' extends the base's host into an attacker-controlled subdomain suffix once concatenated onto a base with no trailing slash. Caught by 0 of the 24 cases that existed before this fix, for the same reason as relative-userinfo-hijack-rejected: nothing in the prior corpus concatenated past the base's own authority.

The anti-vacuity companion to the two authority-extension cases above: a relative input that stays on the base's own origin once concatenated is still accepted, proving the new origin check does not reject every relative input.
A same-origin absolute URL is returned unchanged, query and all — §7 requires the input pass through verbatim on success.
A cross-origin absolute URL is refused, naming both origins in the message.
The same host over a different scheme is a different origin, per §6's origin-tuple definition.
The same host on a different explicit port is a different origin.

An explicit :443 on https is the same origin as none. Python's urlsplit reports the port verbatim where the WHATWG parser elides it, so without the default-port table the bindings disagree on a legitimate pagination link.
The complement, with the default on the base rather than on the input: an explicit :80 on http is the same origin as none.
Scheme and host compare case-insensitively, and the input is still returned in the caller's casing.

An IPv6 host is bracketed in the origin string. Python's urlsplit().hostname strips the brackets and TypeScript's URL.hostname keeps them, so a binding comparing raw hostnames disagrees with the other on every IPv6 base.
Two listeners on one host differ by port alone — the origin change a same-host redirect makes, written down.
Userinfo is ignored: the host of https://api.example.com@evil.com is evil.com. A binding reading the netloc rather than the host accepts this and sends the bearer token to the attacker.

A non-http scheme is absolute and rejected as cross-origin. The startsWith('http') heuristic read this as relative and concatenated it into https://api.example.comftp://evil.com — caught by 0 of the 0 cases that existed before this corpus, and by no test in the TypeScript suite either.
An absolute URL with no host is malformed.
The disclosed edge of §3: 'notes:' is a valid RFC 3986 scheme, so notes:2024/x is absolute and malformed for want of a host rather than being concatenated as a path.
A port that is not a decimal integer is malformed. Python reaches this by the ValueError urlsplit().port raises; TypeScript by new URL throwing.

A raw tab in an absolute URL is malformed. new URL removes U+0009/U+000A/U+000D and fetches the stripped form, so without this rule TypeScript silently fetches a URL the caller never wrote while Python fetches a different one or fails.

A base that is not an absolute URL with a host is refused with its own reason, distinguishing caller misconfiguration from attacker input. Only reachable on the absolute path — §4 never parses the base.
A raw line feed is the second of §5's three forbidden characters. §5 names U+0009, U+000A, and U+000D; a binding that checks only for tab passes the corpus without this case.
A raw carriage return is the third of §5's three forbidden characters. §5 names U+0009, U+000A, and U+000D; a binding that checks only for tab passes the corpus without this case.

§7 requires malformed to be checked before invalid-base. Here both conditions hold at once — the base is not a URL and the input carries forbidden whitespace — so this is the only case that can distinguish the order. A binding that validates its base before inspecting the input reports invalid-base here and fails.

§7 requires invalid-base to be checked before cross-origin. The existing invalid-base case uses an input whose host matches the base's text, so it cannot discriminate order; this one can — a binding comparing origins before validating the base reports cross-origin instead.
